DBSCAN II — Parameters & Reachability

Class 05 taught you what a core, border, and noise point is. It never told you how to actually pick ε and MinPts on real data, or what precise mathematical relationship makes a "cluster" a cluster in the first place. That's this entire class.

01 · revision

ε, MinPts, and the three roles — the whole of Class 05 in one page

Everything below should feel like a fast rewind, not new material. If any one line surprises you, that's exactly the gap this recap exists to close before we build on top of it.

Symbol / termPlain-English meaningFormal definition
ε (epsilon)How far around a point we're willing to looka fixed radius, the same for every point in the dataset
MinPtsHow many points nearby counts as "dense enough"a threshold on the SIZE of a neighborhood
$N_\varepsilon(P)$Everyone within ε of P — P included$\{q \in D \mid d(P,q) \le \varepsilon\}$
CORE pointDense enough on its own — can grow a cluster$|N_\varepsilon(P)| \ge \text{MinPts}$
BORDER pointNot dense on its own, but a passenger of some core pointnot core, but $\in N_\varepsilon$ of some core point
NOISE pointBelongs nowhere — genuinely on its ownnot core, and not in any core point's $N_\varepsilon$
The one asymmetry that explains almost every edge case in this class: only CORE points can pull other points into a cluster. A border point can be pulled in, but it can never do the pulling — its own neighborhood is never even explored. Keep this one sentence loaded; you'll need it constantly today.
02 · nine scenarios, no ambiguity left

Nine cases that resolve every common point of confusion

The three definitions above are simple — but simple rules still produce edge cases people get wrong in practice. Here is genuinely every shape of confusion that comes up, resolved with real numbers.

All nine panels use the SAME ε=1.0 and MinPts=4 (unless a panel says otherwise), so the only thing changing between panels is the geometry — which is exactly the point.

Panels 1–3: the textbook cases

A point with plenty of company is CORE. A point with too little company of its own, but sitting next to a core point, is BORDER. A point with nothing around it at all — not even indirectly reachable — is NOISE. If you only remember three pictures from this whole section, make it these three.

Panels 4–5: the boundary rules, made unambiguous

$|N_\varepsilon(P)| \ge \text{MinPts}$ uses ≥, not > — landing EXACTLY on MinPts still counts as core. Likewise $d(P,q)\le\varepsilon$ uses ≤, not < — a neighbor sitting EXACTLY at distance ε is still inside the neighborhood. Both rules are inclusive at the boundary, and both boundaries occur constantly on real (imperfectly continuous) data.

Panel 6: a pair is not a cluster

Two points can be within ε of EACH OTHER and still both end up as noise — mutual closeness only matters if it pushes $|N_\varepsilon|$ up to MinPts. A pair, a trio — any group smaller than MinPts — is not dense enough to be a seed, no matter how tightly packed that small group is.

Panel 7: the contested border, revisited

A point can be within ε of core points belonging to TWO different clusters at once. It is not core itself, so it can't merge the two clusters — but it will join whichever one reaches it first as the algorithm runs. This is the one truly order-dependent case in all of DBSCAN (Class 05, Case 6).

Panel 8: borders are optional, not mandatory

Nothing says a cluster MUST have border points. If every point in a region already has ≥MinPts neighbors on its own, the whole cluster can be pure core with zero borders — genuinely solid, uniformly dense data produces exactly this.

Panel 9: only core links count, full stop

A point can sit equally close to a noise point and a core point — the noise neighbor contributes nothing, but the single core-point link is enough on its own to make it BORDER. There's no "average" or "majority vote" over neighbors; ONE core connection is sufficient, and non-core neighbors are simply irrelevant to the decision.

03 · the complete procedure, one more time

The DBSCAN algorithm — rewritten cleanly, in pseudocode

Same procedure as Class 05, written twice: once as clean pseudocode you could type into any language, and once as the plain-English walkthrough of what each line is actually doing.

DBSCAN(D, ε, MinPts): # D = dataset, every point starts UNVISITED clusterId = 0 for each point P in D: if P is VISITED: continue mark P as VISITED Neighbors = regionQuery(P, ε) # Nε(P), Section 01 if |Neighbors| < MinPts: label(P) = NOISE # temporary — may be overwritten later continue clusterId += 1 expandCluster(P, Neighbors, clusterId, ε, MinPts) expandCluster(P, Neighbors, clusterId, ε, MinPts): label(P) = clusterId seeds = Neighbors # a queue/seed-set, not yet a fixed list for each point Q in seeds (processed as the queue grows): if Q is UNVISITED: mark Q as VISITED NeighborsQ = regionQuery(Q, ε) if |NeighborsQ| >= MinPts: seeds.append(NeighborsQ) # Q is core too — cluster keeps growing if label(Q) is UNDEFINED or label(Q) == NOISE: label(Q) = clusterId # sweep Q in — as core or as border
1
Pick an unvisited point P, mark it visited, compute $N_\varepsilon(P)$. Every point gets exactly this treatment once — visited is a permanent flag, it never gets unset.
2
Not enough neighbors → label NOISE, but only for now. There is no separate "confirmed noise" bucket anywhere in this algorithm — a NOISE label is just shorthand for "unassigned so far," nothing more.
3
Enough neighbors → P is CORE. Start a new cluster, and load P's entire neighborhood into a seed set — a growing to-do queue, not a fixed list.
4
Process the seed set one point at a time. For each Q: if unvisited, visit it and check if IT is also core — if so, append Q's own neighbors onto the same seed set (the queue keeps growing while it's being consumed). Either way, if Q wasn't already claimed by a cluster, claim it now.
5
Stop when the seed set empties out. That's the entire signal for "this cluster is done" — no core point left in it has anything new to offer.
6
Return to the outer loop, find the next unvisited point, repeat. DBSCAN terminates the moment every point has been visited exactly once.
The one-sentence version: visit a point → if it's dense enough, claim it and everything reachable from it, transitively, through other core points → once nothing new is reachable, that cluster is done → move on. Nothing here needs to know K in advance, and nothing here is random.

See it run — animated, point by point

Same 26-point dataset (two clean, well-separated blobs, plus 2 genuine outliers) run through the exact algorithm above, three separate times, with a different (ε, MinPts) pair each time. Every frame names the point being checked, its neighbor count against MinPts, whether it becomes core / border / noise, and — when a cluster's seed set empties out — exactly why the algorithm stops expanding it. The dashed circle is always $N_\varepsilon$ around the current point; thin lines mark which points fall inside it.

Run 1 — ε too small (ε=0.4, MinPts=3): both real clusters are still found, but ε is too tight to hold each one together — 10 of 26 points (38%) get stranded as noise, even though they're clearly sitting inside a cluster to the eye.
Run 2 — ε and MinPts well chosen (ε=1.1, MinPts=4): both clusters recover cleanly and completely; only the 2 genuine outliers end up noise (8%). This is what "correct" parameters actually look like, point by point.
Run 3 — ε too large (ε=3.0, MinPts=5): ε now reaches all the way across the gap between the two real clusters. Watch the seed set jump from one blob straight into the other — they MERGE into a single cluster, and even both outliers get swallowed in as border points. 0% noise looks good on paper; it's actually the worst result of the three.
The pattern across all three runs: the CORE/BORDER/NOISE mechanic never changes — only ε and MinPts do. Too small and the algorithm becomes too strict, so real cluster members get abandoned as noise. Too large and it becomes too permissive, so genuinely separate clusters get welded into one. This is the exact same trade-off Sections 05–06 walk through with the elbow method — now you've watched it happen point by point instead of just reading the final labels.
04 · the edge case worth dwelling on

What if the very first point you visit is a future border point?

DBSCAN visits points in some order — arbitrary, often just the order they appear in the dataset. That raises an honest question: what happens if a point that will EVENTUALLY be a border point gets checked before the core point that will claim it even exists yet?

Same 14-point dataset as Class 05 (ε=1.5, MinPts=4). A6's final identity never changes — only the TIMING of when it gets recognized does.
1
A6 gets visited early, before any core point of C1 has been discovered yet. DBSCAN has no way of knowing in advance that A6 will later turn out to be a border point — it checks A6 on its own merits, exactly like every other point.
2
$N_\varepsilon(\text{A6}) = \{\text{A4}, \text{A6}\}$ — only 2 points, short of MinPts=4. By the algorithm's own rule (Step 2 above), A6 is labeled NOISE right here.
3
That label is not final — nothing in DBSCAN treats it as final. Re-read Step 4 of the algorithm above: "if Q wasn't already claimed by a cluster, claim it now" — and a temporary NOISE label counts as "not claimed." The door is deliberately left open.
4
Later, A1 is found to be core, and C1 begins expanding through its own seed set: A1 → A2, A3, A5 all get pulled in and checked. A6 is not in $N_\varepsilon(\text{A1})$, so at this point A6 is still sitting there, unrevisited, still labeled noise.
5
Eventually A4 — itself pulled in as part of C1's expansion — gets its OWN neighborhood checked. $N_\varepsilon(\text{A4}) = \{\text{A1,A2,A3,A4,A5,A6}\}$ — and A6 is sitting right there inside it. Step 4 of the algorithm fires: A6's label gets overwritten from NOISE to C1 (as a border point, since A6 itself never reaches MinPts).
The resolving sentence: visiting order can only ever DELAY a point's correct classification — it can never change what that classification eventually is. Whether A6 happens to be checked 1st or 13th in the visiting order, it ends up exactly the same way: BORDER of C1. The final core/border/noise partition of a dataset is a property of the DATA and (ε, MinPts) alone, not of the order the algorithm happens to walk through it.
What genuinely never gets "rescued": a point stays permanently NOISE only if, by the time DBSCAN finishes visiting every single point, NO core point anywhere ever had that point inside its ε-neighborhood. That's a statement about the entire finished dataset, not about any one moment mid-algorithm — which is exactly why the algorithm never commits to a NOISE label until it has literally nothing left to check.
05 · the first knob (optional starting point, not a rule)

Choosing MinPts — where "D+1" and "2D" actually come from

Class 05 treated MinPts as given. It never is, in practice. What follows is exactly what the research literature says — nothing invented on top of it — presented as a starting point for your search, never a requirement you must satisfy.

RuleValue (D = number of features)Source
Absolute floorMinPts ≥ D + 1 (minimum 3)Ester, Kriegel, Sander & Xu (1996) — the original DBSCAN paper
Practical defaultMinPts = 2 × DSander, Ester, Kriegel & Xu (1998) — used in their own worked examples
2D data folkloreMinPts = 4Simply 2×D with D=2 — why "4" shows up constantly in 2D tutorials
Read this table as "here's what the two founding papers actually recommend," not as a derivation. The 1996 paper's own stated reasoning for D+1 is that larger values suppress more noise by requiring more corroborating points before calling something a cluster — smaller values give noise more chances to accidentally look dense. Neither paper claims these numbers are optimal for any particular dataset; both explicitly frame them as starting points for further tuning.

Why the literature suggests D+1 as a floor, and 2D as a better default

The stated logic (Ester et al., 1996) is about suppressing noise: the fewer points you require before calling a region "dense," the more easily a handful of noise points that happen to fall near each other by pure chance can accidentally pass the test and get treated as a real cluster. Requiring at least D+1 points (never fewer than 3, regardless of D) is the paper's own floor for this reason. Sander et al. (1998) then found, empirically, that going further — to 2×D — gave noticeably more robust results across their test data, and used that value in their own examples going forward. Neither paper offers a formal proof that 2×D is optimal; it's an empirically-motivated default, not a theorem.

Is this guaranteed to work on YOUR dataset? No — and neither paper claims it is. Both D+1 and 2×D are generic, dimensionality-based starting points — they know nothing about your data's actual noise level, how many genuine clusters exist, how those clusters' densities compare to each other, or your dataset's size. Treat the table above as "where a reasonable search should begin," never as "the answer."

What are your options when the heuristic doesn't give a good result?

  • Treat 2×D as a starting point, then sweep a small range around it (e.g. from D+1 up through 3×D) and compare outcomes rather than committing to one number blindly.
  • Score each candidate with an internal validity metric — silhouette score computed with noise points EXCLUDED (exactly what the course notebook does) — rather than eyeballing.
  • Look for a STABILITY range, not a single lucky value — the same lesson from Class 05's sensitivity analysis: if MinPts=4,5,6 all give nearly the same cluster count and noise %, that plateau is trustworthy in a way a single isolated value never is.
  • Let domain knowledge overrule the formula outright — if your business definition of "a real cluster" requires at least 8 linked transactions to matter, MinPts=8 is the right answer regardless of what 2×D says.
  • Scale MinPts UP for larger or noisier datasets — more points means more opportunities for noise to randomly cluster together by chance, so bigger, messier data generally wants a somewhat larger MinPts than the bare formula suggests.
  • If clusters in your data genuinely have very different densities from each other, no single MinPts (paired with any single ε) will serve all of them well — that's not a tuning failure, it's a structural limitation of DBSCAN itself (Section 13 comes back to this, with HDBSCAN as the fix).
06 · the second knob

Choosing ε — the k-distance / elbow method

MinPts chosen first (Section 05). Now: for THAT MinPts, what radius ε actually matches the real density structure of this dataset, instead of being a guess?

One thing that looks odd here: Section 01 said a core point needs Nε(P) ≥ MinPts, and Nε(P) counts P itself. So why does step 1 below say "MinPts-th nearest neighbor," not "(MinPts−1)-th"? Section 07 gives the one, single reason right after this section — worth reading before you teach this part.

The construction, step by step

1
For every single point $x_i$ in the dataset, compute $d_i$ = the distance to its MinPts-th nearest neighbor — counting $x_i$ itself as sitting at distance 0, rank 1, so this genuinely reaches out to MinPts−1 real OTHER points.
2
Collect ALL of these distances — one number per point — and sort them in ascending order, smallest to largest.
3
Plot the sorted values. This is the "k-distance plot" (k here is MinPts). Look for a "knee" — a point near the right-hand end where the curve suddenly bends upward from a long, flat run into a steep climb.
4
Read the y-value at the knee. That value is your candidate ε.
Left: real two-cluster-plus-noise data — a genuine knee exists near the right edge. Right: uniformly scattered data with no natural break — the curve climbs smoothly throughout, and there is no knee to find.

Why does the knee actually make a GOOD ε — not just a convenient-looking bend?

Think about what the y-axis value means for any one point: "how far do I have to reach out to find MinPts−1 real companions?" A point buried deep inside a genuine dense cluster has a SMALL such distance — its neighbors are right there. A point that's noise, or on the sparse fringe of a cluster, has to reach much FARTHER to scrape together the same number of companions — a LARGE distance. Sorting ascending puts all the "didn't have to reach far" (cluster-core-like) points on the left, as a long flat run, and all the "had to reach far" (noise-like) points on the right, where the curve climbs steeply. The knee is precisely the boundary between these two populations — it's not an arbitrary bend, it's the data telling you where "genuinely dense" stops and "genuinely sparse" begins. Setting ε at that value means: every point whose natural neighborhood is at least that dense will pass the MinPts test; every point sparser than that will correctly fail it.

What if no elbow comes — the curve is smooth, "all short," no knee anywhere?

This is not a failure of the method — it's the method correctly reporting that your data has no single natural density threshold. It happens when density varies CONTINUOUSLY across the dataset rather than jumping between two distinct regimes (dense cluster vs. sparse noise) — imagine population density fading gradually from a city center outward, with no genuine edge to the city, rather than a city block sitting next to open farmland. In that situation, any ε you pick is somewhat arbitrary, because the data itself doesn't contain a natural cut point.

  • Check for a subtle (not absent) elbow first — a numerical curvature/"kneedle" detector often finds a real knee that's just too gentle to eyeball confidently.
  • Fall back to the stability-range method from Class 05 §07 — sweep a handful of candidate ε values and pick the range where the number of clusters and the noise % stay stable, rather than searching for one perfect number that may not exist.
  • Let the problem's own units define ε directly — "two customers are the same segment if they're within 50 rupees of spend and 2 days of recency" is a perfectly valid way to set ε, bypassing the geometric search entirely.
  • Always double-check feature scaling first — an apparently elbow-less curve is sometimes an ARTIFACT of one unscaled feature (e.g. raw rupee amounts next to a 0–1 ratio) dominating every distance calculation. Standardizing features (as the course notebook does before computing distances) can reveal a real elbow that unscaled data was hiding.
  • Accept that a single global ε may be the wrong tool for this dataset. The next example shows exactly when that happens — and it isn't fixable by tuning harder.

Where the whole method breaks down: clusters of genuinely different densities

Every trick above assumes there's ONE good ε waiting to be found. Sometimes there genuinely isn't — not because you haven't searched hard enough, but because the dataset itself contains clusters that are honestly, structurally different in density from each other.

Same 180-point dataset (real scikit-learn DBSCAN output, not sketched) in all three panels: two tight, dense groups plus one loose, spread-out group of the same size.

Set ε small enough to keep the two dense groups correctly separate, and the sparse group — which is just as real a cluster, only spread over more space — shatters into noise and fragments. Set ε large enough to recover the sparse group cleanly, and the two dense groups, which were always close together, MERGE into one. There is no third value of ε that fixes both problems at once, because the two failure modes come from the SAME knob moving in the SAME direction — you cannot simultaneously make ε small (for the dense pair) and large (for the sparse group).

The honest conclusion: DBSCAN, with one global ε and one global MinPts, does not work well on data whose real clusters have meaningfully different densities from each other. This isn't a parameter-search problem you can tune your way out of — it's a structural property of the algorithm. (Section 13 picks this back up with HDBSCAN, which is built specifically to remove this limitation.)
07 · a correction, and the one reason

Why MinPts, not MinPts−1, in the elbow plot

A correction, and an apology: an earlier version of these notes explained this exact point in a way that wasn't precise enough, and it caused real confusion in class. That confusion was on the handwritten notes. What follows is the one, exact, correct explanation — please use this version going forward, in place of anything said earlier.
If your neighbor search……then ask for
Includes the point itself (query the dataset against itself — this course's method)the MinPts-th nearest neighbor
Excludes the point itself entirelythe (MinPts − 1)-th nearest OTHER point

The one combination that is WRONG, and the exact source of the confusion: excluding the point itself, but still asking for the MinPts-th nearest OTHER point. That silently asks for one real neighbor more than the core rule needs. This course always uses row 1 — Section 06's steps ask for the MinPts-th nearest neighbor precisely because the search includes the point itself.

Now, the full reasoning behind that table, stated exactly: Section 01 said a core point needs $|N_\varepsilon(P)| \ge \text{MinPts}$, and $N_\varepsilon(P)$ counts P itself. So the REAL requirement on other points is only MinPts−1 of them. Then why does Section 06 go looking for the MinPts-th nearest neighbor, instead of the (MinPts−1)-th? Here is the one chain of reasoning that answers it — four steps, no alternate conventions, no hedging.

1
What the core rule actually needs. $|N_\varepsilon(P)| \ge \text{MinPts}$, and P itself is always inside $N_\varepsilon(P)$ (its distance to itself is 0, which is always ≤ ε). So out of those MinPts required points, ONE of them is P. That leaves MinPts − 1 as the number of REAL other points P needs nearby. This part you already knew — it's just the target number we're aiming for.
2
How the neighbor search actually works. To build the elbow plot, we ask a nearest-neighbor search "who is closest to P?" — searching the WHOLE dataset, which includes P. And P's distance to itself is always exactly 0, the smallest possible distance there is. So P is always returned as its own closest match, unconditionally, for every single point, every single time. There's no avoiding it — that's just what "search the whole dataset" means.
3
Put those two facts together. The search's very first result is always a throwaway — P finding itself. So if you ask this search for only (MinPts−1) neighbors, you'd get P itself PLUS only (MinPts−2) real others — one short of the MinPts−1 you actually needed from Step 1!
4
The fix. To end up with MinPts−1 real neighbors from a search that always burns its first result on P itself, you have to ask for one MORE than MinPts−1 — which is exactly MinPts. P eats result #1 for free; results #2 through #MinPts are the MinPts−1 real neighbors you were after all along. That's the entire reason. "MinPts" in the elbow method isn't a different number from Section 01's MinPts−1 — it's the same MinPts−1 real neighbors, plus the one throwaway slot P's self-match always costs you.
A real point P from Section 06's dataset (MinPts=5). Slot 1 is always P finding itself, for free, at distance 0. Slots 2–5 are the 4 real neighbors the core rule actually needs (MinPts−1=4). Ask for 5 total, and you land exactly on the right boundary — ε = 0.135.
08–10 · the three relations, made simple

Directly density-reachable, density-reachable, density-connected

These three ideas sound formal, but they're really just one small story told three ways. Picture a party: a core point is a host — someone with enough people already standing around them that they're allowed to personally invite others in. A border point is a guest — someone who got invited, but doesn't have enough people around them to invite anyone else themselves. That's the whole picture. Everything below is just: who can invite whom, and how far does an invite chain reach?

Directly density-reachable — "can p personally invite q?"

In plain words: p can directly invite q into the cluster if TWO things are both true — p is a host (core point), and q is standing close enough to hear the invite (within ε). If either one fails, the invite doesn't happen.
formal definition$q$ is directly density-reachable from $p$ iff (a) $q \in N_\varepsilon(p)$, and (b) $p$ is core ($|N_\varepsilon(p)| \ge \text{MinPts}$).
Every shape this can take: works both ways when both are hosts, works one way only when one is a guest, fails if they're too far apart, fails if the "inviter" isn't a host at all — and two guests of the same host still can't invite each other.

Worked example (ε=1.5, MinPts=4): A4 → A6 works, because A4 is a host (core) and A6 is close enough. Flip it — A6 → A4 — and it fails immediately: A6 is just a guest, so it isn't allowed to invite anyone, no matter how close A4 is standing.

The one rule to remember: only hosts can invite. A guest can be invited, but a guest can never do the inviting — which means two guests of the SAME host still can't invite each other directly (panel 6). That gap is exactly what "density-connected" fixes, two sections from now.

Density-reachable — "can q trace an invite chain back to p?"

In plain words: q is density-reachable from p if there's a chain of direct invites connecting them — p invites p2, p2 (if also a host) invites p3, and so on, until someone in the chain invites q. One hop or many hops, it still counts, as long as every link in the chain is a valid direct invite.
formal definition$q$ is density-reachable from $p$ if a chain $p{=}p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n{=}q$ exists where each $p_{i+1}$ is directly reachable from $p_i$.
A short 2-hop chain, a longer 5-hop chain tracing a curve, a chain that snaps the moment one link is a guest instead of a host, two separate groups no chain can bridge, and noise no chain can ever reach.

Worked example: B5 is too far from B1 for a direct invite. But B1 (host) invites B3 (also a host), and B3 invites B5 — a 2-hop chain. So B5 IS density-reachable from B1, just not directly.

Why this matters: it's how DBSCAN handles curvy, non-round clusters. A crescent shape can have two ends that are far apart in a straight line, but if a chain of hosts runs along the curve connecting them, the two ends still count as reachable (panel 2). And the same one rule from before still applies: a guest can never start a chain, however short (panel 5).

Density-connected — "do p and q share a host, even if neither invited the other?"

In plain words: two guests, X and Y, might never invite each other — neither is a host, so neither CAN invite. But if they were both personally invited by the same host O, we still say they belong at the same party. That shared host is all "density-connected" means.
formal definition$p$ and $q$ are density-connected if some point $o$ exists such that both $p$ and $q$ are density-reachable from $o$.
Two guests glued by one shared host, a whole ring of guests glued by one hub, two hosts linked by a chain of hosts in between, two separate parties with no shared host, and nearby noise that still doesn't count.

Worked example: O is a host, and X and Y are both its guests on opposite sides — each directly invited by O, but too far apart (and not hosts themselves) to ever invite each other. They're still density-connected, through O.

Why you need this third idea at all: without it, there'd be no way to say "X and Y are at the same party" when neither can reach the other directly. Density-connectedness is what glues an entire cluster into one group, guests included — it's the relation that actually matches "same cluster."

Putting all three side by side

PairDirectly reachable?Reachable (any # hops)?Density-connected?Verdict
A4 → A6YESYESYESSame cluster (C1)
A6 → A4NO (A6 not core)NOYES (via A4)Same cluster (C1) — connectedness saves it
B1 → B5NOYES (via B3)YESSame cluster (C2)
X ↔ Y (custom eg.)NONOYES (via O)Same cluster
A1 ↔ B1NONONODifferent clusters — no relation holds, and none should
A1 → N1NONONON1 is noise — no core point's neighborhood ever contains it

The last two rows matter as much as the first four: when NONE of the three relations hold between two points, that's not a gap in the theory — it's the theory correctly telling you those points don't belong together (different clusters), or that one of them is genuinely noise.

11 · connecting theory back to practice

Why DBSCAN actually needs all three of these terms

These aren't academic decoration bolted onto an already-working algorithm. They're the reason the algorithm is provably doing something coherent at all.

They give DBSCAN a real, formal definition of "cluster"

The 1996 DBSCAN paper doesn't define a cluster as "whatever the seed-set expansion procedure happens to output." It defines a cluster as: a maximal set of points that are pairwise density-CONNECTED, where every point density-REACHABLE from any point already in the set is also required to be in the set (maximality). The algorithm from Section 03 is a practical, efficient way to COMPUTE exactly this mathematically defined object — it isn't an ad hoc heuristic that happens to look reasonable.

They explain the core/border asymmetry rigorously

"Only core points can expand a cluster" (Section 01's one-sentence rule) is really just direct density-reachability's asymmetry, restated. Once you have the formal relation, the procedural rule falls out of it automatically — you don't need to memorize it as a separate fact.

Reachability is WHY arbitrary shapes work at all

A crescent, a spiral, a ring — none of these have points that are all mutually within ε of each other. What makes them ONE cluster is a continuous chain of directly-reachable hops threading along the actual shape. Without the formal notion of (multi-hop) density-reachability, there would be no principled way to say a crescent is "one cluster" at all.

Density-connectedness is WHY border points on opposite sides still merge

Two border points on opposite edges of the same round blob are typically NOT within ε of each other, and neither can reach the other (border points can't reach anything). Without density-connectedness as a distinct, symmetric relation, the formal definition of "cluster" would have no way to include both of them in the same set — yet intuitively, and in the algorithm's actual output, they obviously belong together.

The one sentence to walk away with: core/border/noise tells you what a POINT is; directly-reachable, reachable, and connected tell you what a CLUSTER is, formally and rigorously — and the algorithm from Section 03 is simply the efficient recipe for computing that formal definition without ever explicitly building the full reachability graph.
12 · what DBSCAN gets right

Advantages of DBSCAN

No K, ever

The number of clusters emerges entirely from the density structure of the data — you never specify it in advance, unlike K-Means, K-Means++, Hierarchical, or GMM.

Genuinely arbitrary cluster shapes

Crescents, rings, spirals — anything a continuous chain of density-reachable points can trace. This follows directly from Section 09's multi-hop reachability, not from any assumption about shape.

Noise is first-class, not forced

Every other algorithm in this module must assign every point to some cluster. DBSCAN is the first willing to say "this point genuinely belongs nowhere" — critical for fraud detection, outlier flagging, and real messy data.

Outliers don't distort the clusters

K-Means and GMM centroids/means get dragged by a single extreme outlier. DBSCAN just labels that point noise — the shape of the real clusters is untouched.

Only two hyperparameters

ε and MinPts — and Sections 05–07 gave you principled (if imperfect) ways to choose both, rather than pure guesswork.

Mostly deterministic

No random initialization to get unlucky with, unlike K-Means/K-Means++/GMM. The only non-determinism is the rare Case-6 contested border point (Section 02, panel 7) — a small, well-understood, documented edge case.

13 · what DBSCAN gets wrong

Limitations of DBSCAN — and a first look at HDBSCAN

One global ε and MinPts assumes roughly uniform density

If one real cluster is dense and another is genuinely sparse, a single (ε, MinPts) pair cannot serve both — it will either shatter the sparse cluster into noise or merge the dense one into a blob (Class 05 §07's sensitivity analysis showed exactly this trade-off).

The curse of dimensionality

In high-dimensional spaces, distances between points concentrate — everything starts looking roughly equidistant — which makes both ε and MinPts far harder to choose meaningfully, and Nε(P) loses its discriminative power.

Parameter choice is a genuine search, not a formula

D+1, 2×D, and the k-distance elbow (Sections 05–06) are guides, not guarantees — real, messy, differently-scaled data can defeat all three simultaneously, and feature scaling matters enormously since ε is a raw distance threshold.

A single flat partition, not a hierarchy

One (ε, MinPts) pair gives you ONE clustering. You don't get to see how clusters would merge or split at other density thresholds without rerunning the whole algorithm repeatedly by hand.

A high-level hint of HDBSCAN

HDBSCAN = Hierarchical DBSCAN. Instead of committing to one global ε upfront, it conceptually runs DBSCAN across EVERY possible ε value at once, builds a hierarchy of how clusters nest, merge, and split as the density threshold changes, and then automatically extracts the clusters that are the most STABLE across that entire hierarchy.

What this buys you: HDBSCAN can find a tight, dense cluster AND a loose, sparse cluster in the SAME dataset, each at its own natural density level — precisely the "one global ε can't serve everyone" limitation above, solved directly. It also typically needs just one main parameter (roughly, a minimum cluster size) rather than two, since it no longer has to guess a single ε at all.

The trade-off: HDBSCAN is more complex internally (it builds a minimum spanning tree and a condensed cluster hierarchy under the hood) and somewhat heavier computationally. For data with roughly uniform density throughout, plain DBSCAN remains simpler and just as effective — HDBSCAN earns its extra complexity specifically when density genuinely varies across your clusters.

14 · everything in one page

DBSCAN II: the complete picture

1

MinPts ≥ D+1, or 2×D — optional starting points

Both numbers come straight from the two founding papers' own noise-suppression reasoning, not from a proof — treat them as where to START a search, never as a rule you must satisfy.

2

ε comes from the k-distance knee

Sort each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbor in ASCENDING order (smallest to largest) — the knee near the right-hand end separates dense-cluster points from sparse/noise ones.

3

Self-inclusion is bookkeeping, not conflict

d(P,P)=0 always — Nε(P) counts it because it's a pure count; the elbow plot excludes it because a constant zero carries no density information.

4

Three relations, one purpose

Directly-reachable (one hop), reachable (chained hops), connected (shared ancestor) — together they formally define what a "cluster" is, borders included.

5

Visiting order only ever delays, never changes

A border point checked before its cluster's first core point is found gets temporarily mislabeled noise — and correctly reclassified the moment a core point's expansion reaches it.

6

Uniform density is the one assumption left

A single global (ε, MinPts) can't serve clusters of very different densities at once — that's precisely the gap HDBSCAN closes.

The one-sentence mental model for this whole class

Class 05 taught you to recognize density. Class 06 taught you to formally define it, choose its thresholds with evidence instead of guesswork, and prove — rigorously, not just procedurally — that the algorithm's output is exactly the mathematically "correct" answer.
